I had to get braces as an adult after having two wisdom teeth removed, because my teeth had too much space and became separated. However my wisdom teeth were damaging my other teeth, and one had become impacted.

After that, I was really afraid of getting the other two removed, and I put it off until I ended up with an infection in my jaw that progressed very rapidly until I needed a root canal (which was the worst toothache I've ever had and cost a fortune). I was told for about 15 years my wisdom teeth should come out, but weren't causing a problem, so the decision was mine. I said, nah, leave them. Fast forward to about 3 years ago and they were nudging nearby teeth and I was developing a gum infection. So, it went from "you should think about taking them out" to "you should take them out before they permanently screw up your nearby molars."

However, I was older when I had them removed, and the older you are the more chance for complications. I wound up with dry socket and a permanently damaged nerve where I can't feel the lower right side of my face. Dry socket was painful but it was managed. The numbness on the other hand...

Had I taken them out when I was younger, the chances for those complications would have been lower. Much regret.

My dentist says it's because they can be hard to clean once they've broken through the gums. It can lead to cavities and infection, so although it isn't bothering you now it's more of a preventative measure to take them out.

This is my situation. My top wisdom teeth have come in on both sides. I don't have any on the bottom. The top ones have plenty of room so they didn't mess up my other teeth, but they sit so far back that they are hard to clean and tend to accumulate more food around them. Getting to the back of them makes me gag sometimes. I'll probably have to get them pulled once they start getting cavities which I'm sure they will since I know I'm not cleaning them as well as my other teeth.
Its very hard to clean them, which leads to decay and they can cause crowding problems in the future.

So, one of the biggest issues that can be caused is the fact that your wisdom teeth are so far back. I had 2 of mine growing in normally, however, it was impossible to brush. The dentist made me get them removed because at my point in life, it's easier(though it would have been easier to do it 9 years ago) than later down the road when they started to cause real issues. It's proactive solution.

There are a few things that could happen if you leave your wisdom teeth in:

  • Creates a impossible to clean gap in your mouth causing bacteria infection (this hurts.. a lot -- also, imagine making out with someone with a bacteria infection they don't know about. Not fun.)

  • Higher chance of tooth decay(cavities) in areas near your jaw, caused by the increased difficulty for brushing and flossing the area... this also hurts a lot.

  • Can decrease the space between your other teeth, making hard to reach places along your entire mouth. Causing tooth decay^

  • Can grow impacted, which will alter the look of your face... and eventually hurt a lot (this is a common theme)
  • The wisdom tooth root can grow nearly indefinitely, and can literally straddle your nerve along your jaw. If left unchecked, it can cause you to lose feeling on your lips. Also, it makes it extremely difficult to remove if it gets to this point and you may lose feeling in your lip anyway. This is permanent.
  • Overgrown wisdom teeth can also cause sinus damage. (This is probably the worst.)
  • Overgrown wisdom teeth can also inflame your gums and swell, making it hard to brush. This is very bloody.
  • Impacted wisdom teeth can cause alignment issues causing you to require braces, also it can reverse the effects of braces or any other type of dental work done previously. Unbalanced teeth alignment can cause seriously jaw stress in your later years. (I have this problem, it sucks).

Wisdom teeth removal is a preventative procedure, it may not be necessary for you, but there are higher risks than rewards for keeping them in. Get it done earlier and it will be quick and somewhat painless (in comparison). Leave them in and you'll have multiple nightmares to deal with. I'm an example of someone who didn't get their wisdom teeth removal during my late teens, I had to go through 2 years of dental work to make it just not hurt anymore.

My favorite one is Chicken in a Hunters sauce. The French name escapes me at the moment but essentially here is the recipe:

Ingredients: pinch of Salt/Pepper

1 piece favorite cut of chicken (preferably skin on, bone removed but your preference)

1/4 cup small dice carrots (or other root vegetable, turnips go great as well)

1/4 cup small dice onion

1/4 cup small dice celery

1 Roma tomato thinly sliced (or about 1/4 cup of your favorite mater!)

1 tablespoon high quality mustard (stone ground Dijon is my choice)

Aromatics (garlic, rosemary, sage, oregano, herbs de Provence; that's my go to but don't feel constrained)

Equipment:

One plate for holding raw chicken

One 12" or around there stainless steel pan (oven safe would save on dishes)

Whisk

Tongs

Method: 1.In a stainless steel sauté pan heat until water dances across the surface (med high?, the pan needs to be almost smoking)

  1. Take that pinch of salt and pepper and rub it on the skin side of the chicken, if no skin just pick a side.

  2. Evenly and quickly lay chicken salt/pepper side down on pan (note: I didn't say oil the pan because we want that chicken to stick to a certain degree. The resulting liquid/carmelization that develops on the bottom of the pan will be the base of the hunters sauce. It is also important to not disturb the chicken for several minutes, don't let it burn but if you start fudging with it the skin won't crisp evenly)

  3. After a few minutes, or when you can smell cooked chicken in the air, flip the piece of chicken and just sear the bottom. You want to actually finish cooking the chicken in the sauce. Remove the chicken and place on the plate for the time being.

  4. IMPORTANT STEP: immediately drain the chicken fat and all remaining juices from the pan. I give it to my dog, but you could give it to your coworker, tee hee. The fat will actually destabilize the sauce and add way to much chicken flavor.

  5. Turn down the heat to say a medium low and put the pan back on the heat. When the pan begins to smoke just slightly or all of the delicious chicken stuck to the pan turn a golden brown throw them maters in there and start scraping with the whisk! It should come off pretty quickly but add a 1/4 cup of water to help things get stirred.

  6. Add the celery, carrots, onions plus your aromatics and keep stirring! Once all the chicken is dissolved in the liquid you can let it set on simmer stirring occasionally to ensure the sauce isnt burning.

  7. After the carrots begin to get soft throw the mustard in there and whisk furiously until everything's ice and blended. Congratulations! You have just made a classical French sauce!!!

  8. Plop the chicken back in the sauce salt/pepper sode up and just let everything simmer till the chicken is cooking. I like to leave the skin on and baste it until its done then put it under the broil until the chicken skin+sauce get a nice crisp and beautiful color. But that can be Tricky if you aren't used to using a broiler, so it's up to you.

  9. Boom your done, season to taste but I find that I hardly ever need to add salt. I usually eat this with a nice sharp vinaigrette on a an arugula salad. Offsets the heaviness of the chicken, but anything neutral works as well like rice, quinoa, etc. Usually takes about 30 Minutes from start to Finnish but depends on how much chicken your cooking, pan size and the such.

Enjoy!

It's quite good! Not super complicated either, this was kind of the chicken and dumplings of french renaissance era. Plus you make a protein and vegetable based gravy instead of using wheat. I love my wheat and wheat accessories but with this method it's unnecessary and cuts useless simple carbs.

Piggybacking on your comment: Spot fat reduction isn't a viable option. In other words OP, you can't pick a spot and lose fat. Where your body stores fat first and burns it off first is largely determined by genetics. That said, you can lose fat in general, and when you lose enough - eventually your body will lose it around your stomach. For me personally, when I put on weight it goes to my ass, my love handles, and then my belly in that order.

Track your caloric intake, everything you eat for two weeks. Get a cheap food scale. Weigh what you eat, calculate the calories and ideally the macronutrients as well. After 2 weeks you'll have a decent library of what you usually eat and you won't have to measure and math so much anymore.

Take that info and compare it against an online TDEE calculator. To lose weight, you just have to output more calories than you input - I would recommend starting at a 200 cal deficit and work from there. Typically you want to keep your proteins up, and cut cals from other things like carbs/sugar and fat. After 2 or 3 weeks of eating to your calorie goal, check you weight again: If you're losing weight, you're doing great. If you are at the same weight or heavier, cut another 200 cals. Rinse, repeat the process again in another 2 weeks.

Basically, your body is going to become your own science experiment. Test, experiment, and measure your results. Then tweak your inputs. You'll refine your experiment over time and you WILL improve if you keep at it. It's actually kind of fun.

If you want to lose weight, you'll need to reduce your calories. Though I wouldn't decrease protein consumption, because relatively high protein has a number of benefits if you're trying to preserve muscle. Additionally, the hypothesis has been presented that low protein may cause greater hunger (known as the 'protein leverage' hypothesis).

As others have said, spot reduction is largely impossible. However, there is a possible link between excessive cortisol levels and elevated fat, particularly visceral fat, though this would suggest more of a 'beer belly' than 'love handles' (visceral fat crowds the organs behind the abdominal wall). Either way, reducing cortisol levels would involve reducing stress and getting more restful sleep. Making those changes could make the fat less 'stubborn', but calorie deficits are stressful to the body, so there's a balancing act embedded in this theory.

Also, you can check yourself of anterior pelvic tilt.

Lastly, I'd be remiss if I didn't say that you'd be surprised at how a little extra muscle can make the same amount of fat (or even more) appear to be less. Pursuant to that rationale, you could instead switch to a barbell training routine to build on your lean body mass, using more of a 'recomp' or a 'clean bulk' dietary strategy.

Any way you go about losing it, best of luck.
